# Life cycles and vectors

> *A child swallows worm eggs from soil, and a traveller is bitten by a mosquito that carries the
> malaria parasite. In both, the parasite's life cycle sets where it is caught, which stage causes
> disease, which stage is found in the laboratory, and where control can break the cycle.*

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Learning objectives
- Distinguish protozoa from helminths by whether they multiply inside the human host, and explain
  what that means for the size of an infection.
- Define definitive host, intermediate host, and biological and mechanical vector, and identify each
  in the life cycle of *Plasmodium falciparum*.
- Sort parasites by the route by which they reach humans, and name the stage that enters by each
  route.
- Read a life cycle to say where a parasite is caught, which stage causes disease, which stage is
  found in the laboratory and where control can break the cycle.
- Choose the sample in which a parasite can be found, and explain when in the infection it appears
  there.
- Relate drugs against parasites to what parasites have and human cells lack.
:::

## Two kinds of parasite {#sec-life-kinds}

In medical microbiology, the word **parasite** usually refers to a protozoan or a helminth: a
eukaryote that lives on or in a host at the host's expense. **Protozoa** are single-celled eukaryotes
that move and feed independently. **Helminths** are parasitic worms, many-celled animals that develop
from the egg into the adult through immature stages called **larvae** (singular larva). The anchors
are *Plasmodium falciparum*, a protozoan, and *Ascaris lumbricoides*, a helminth
(see the six questions answered for both in [*The microbial
world*](../foundations/microbial-world.qmd#sec-world-six)).

The two kinds differ in one property that shapes every infection they cause: whether the parasite
multiplies inside the human host.

| | Protozoa | Helminths |
|---|---|---|
| Built from | One eukaryotic cell | A many-celled animal with tissues and organs |
| Multiply inside the human host? | Yes, by repeated division | With few exceptions, no: the eggs or larvae they produce must leave the host before they can infect anyone |
| The size of an infection depends on | How far the parasite multiplies before the host controls it | How many eggs or larvae entered the body |

A protozoan can therefore turn a small inoculum, the number of organisms received (see [*Microbes
and their hosts*](../foundations/host-microbe.qmd#sec-host-factors)), into a large infection.

::: {.example}
A mosquito injects only a small number of *P. falciparum* parasites, but each one that reaches the
liver gives rise to thousands, and these go on multiplying in red blood cells.
:::

A helminth infection is instead the sum of a person's exposures. Each adult *A. lumbricoides* in the
intestine develops from one swallowed egg, and the eggs it lays leave in the faeces, so the number of
worms, and the harm they do, rise with the number of eggs swallowed (see
[*Helminths*](helminths.qmd)). A few helminths can add to their own numbers inside the host.

::: {.example}
One is *Strongyloides stercoralis*, a roundworm that enters through the skin: its larvae can become
infective inside the gut and reinfect the same person, so an infection can persist for decades after
the person has left the place where it was caught (see [*Helminths*](helminths.qmd)).
:::

Medically important protozoa are grouped by where in the body they live, and helminths by body form
(see [*Protozoa*](protozoa.qmd) and [*Helminths*](helminths.qmd)).

## Hosts, vectors and routes {#sec-life-hosts}

### Hosts and vectors {#sec-life-vectors}

Many parasites live in more than one host during their life cycle, and each host is named by what the
parasite does in it:

- The **definitive host** is the host in which the parasite reproduces sexually.
- An **intermediate host** is a host in which the parasite develops or multiplies without reproducing
  sexually.
- A **vector** is an arthropod that carries an organism between hosts (see [*Transmission, outbreaks
  and One Health*](../foundations/transmission-outbreaks.qmd#sec-trans-routes)).

A vector carries a parasite in one of two ways. In a **biological vector** the parasite develops or
multiplies, and the vector cannot pass it on until it has done so. A **mechanical vector** carries an
organism on its body or mouthparts, unchanged. A parasite that needs a biological vector is therefore
found only where that vector can live.

::: {.example}
In the life cycle of *P. falciparum*, sexual reproduction takes place in the mosquito, so the
mosquito is both the definitive host and a biological vector; humans, in whom the parasite
multiplies only asexually, are the intermediate host.
:::

::: {.example}
A housefly that walks on faeces and then on food can carry worm eggs on its legs and mouthparts;
nothing develops in the fly, so it is a mechanical vector.
:::

*A. lumbricoides* has neither a vector nor an intermediate host: humans are its definitive host, and
its eggs complete their development in soil. Many other helminths do pass through an intermediate
host, and for several of them humans are the definitive host.

::: {.example}
The *Taenia* tapeworms live as adults in the human intestine, so humans are their definitive host;
pigs or cattle are their intermediate hosts, carrying the larvae in cysts in their muscle (see
[*Helminths*](helminths.qmd)).
:::

### How parasites reach humans {#sec-life-routes}

The stage that enters a person is built for its route. Most parasites that are swallowed have first
survived outside the body, as a helminth egg or as a **cyst**, a resistant stage that survives outside
the body and is the infective form of many protozoa. A parasite that enters through the skin does so
as a larva that can pierce it, and one carried by a vector enters as a stage that has developed inside
the vector. Parasites reach humans by five routes (the organisms named are described in
[*Protozoa*](protozoa.qmd) and [*Helminths*](helminths.qmd)):

::: {.concept-tree}
[How parasites reach humans]{.tree-title}

- Swallowed
  - Cysts in water or food contaminated with faeces: *Giardia duodenalis*
  - Eggs that have matured in soil contaminated with faeces, carried to the mouth on hands or raw
    vegetables: *A. lumbricoides*
  - Larval cysts in undercooked meat: *Taenia* tapeworms, in pork or beef
- Through the skin
  - Larvae in soil contaminated with faeces: hookworms, through bare feet
  - Larvae in fresh water: schistosomes, through the skin of people who wade, bathe or swim
- The bite of a vector: *P. falciparum*, injected by a mosquito
- Sexual contact: *Trichomonas vaginalis*
- Across the placenta: *Toxoplasma gondii*, in a first infection during pregnancy
:::

The route predicts where a parasite is common and how it can be prevented. Parasites swallowed in
material contaminated with faeces, or entering through the skin from soil, are common where
sanitation is poor, and a parasite carried by a vector is found only where its vector lives.

## Reading a life cycle {#sec-life-reading}

A life cycle shows each stage of a parasite and where that stage lives. We read it with four
questions:

1. Where is it caught: which stage infects people, and where is that stage found?
2. Which stage causes disease?
3. Which stage is found in the laboratory, and in which sample?
4. Where can control break the cycle?

### *Plasmodium falciparum*: the worked example {#sec-life-falciparum}

*P. falciparum* passes between people in the bite of a female *Anopheles* mosquito; only female
mosquitoes feed on blood. The stage the mosquito injects is the **sporozoite**, which travels in the
blood to the liver.

::: {.flow}
1. A bite injects sporozoites
2. They multiply in liver cells, without symptoms
3. New parasites invade red blood cells
4. Repeated multiplication bursts red cells, with fever
5. Some become male and female sexual forms
6. A mosquito takes them up; sexual reproduction in its gut
7. Sporozoites reach its salivary glands
:::

The cycle closes when the mosquito bites again.

*Anopheles* mosquitoes bite mainly at night and pick up the parasite from infected people, so
falciparum malaria is caught where both are found: mostly in sub-Saharan Africa, and in parts of Asia
and South America. Most malaria diagnosed in Singapore is acquired abroad, so a history of travel is
the main clue. Because the cycle in red cells can continue on its own, the parasite can also pass in
transfused blood, without a mosquito or a liver stage.

Only the blood stage causes disease. The liver stage causes no symptoms, so illness begins no sooner
than about a week after the bite. In the blood, each cycle of multiplication ends with the infected
red cells bursting, and material set free from them stimulates the host's white blood cells to
release signals that cause fever. The destruction of red cells causes anaemia, and red cells infected with
*P. falciparum* also stick to the walls of small blood vessels, the basis of severe falciparum
malaria (see [*Protozoa*](protozoa.qmd)). The sexual forms cause no symptoms.

The blood stage is also the one the laboratory finds. A stained blood film shows the parasites inside
red cells and how many cells are infected, and an antigen test detects a parasite protein in a drop
of blood, on a paper strip, within minutes. Early in the illness the parasites may be too few to see,
so a single negative film does not exclude malaria, and the film is repeated while malaria is still
suspected.

Control can break the cycle at the mosquito, at infected people and at the person at risk. Bed nets
treated with insecticide stop mosquitoes biting at night, and insecticide sprayed on the inside walls
of homes kills mosquitoes that rest there after feeding; prompt treatment reduces the number of people whose blood can infect mosquitoes; and
drugs taken by travellers prevent disease. Vaccines that act against the sporozoite, the stage the
mosquito injects, are now given to young children in parts of Africa and give partial protection.

### *Ascaris lumbricoides*: a cycle without a vector {#sec-life-ascaris}

The cycle of *A. lumbricoides* passes through soil instead of a vector:

::: {.flow}
1. Eggs pass in faeces
2. Weeks in warm, moist soil make them infective
3. Swallowed eggs hatch in the gut
4. Larvae cross the gut wall and travel through the liver to the lungs
5. Larvae are coughed up and swallowed
6. Adults mature in the small intestine
:::

Freshly passed eggs cannot infect anyone until they have spent weeks in soil, so the worm does not
pass directly from person to person. The source of infection is soil contaminated with faeces, in
which the eggs survive for months, and the eggs reach the mouth on hands or on raw vegetables grown in
that soil. The adults do not multiply in the intestine, so every adult comes from one swallowed egg.

Set side by side, the two anchors give different answers to every question:

| Question | *P. falciparum* | *A. lumbricoides* |
|---|---|---|
| Where is it caught? | From the bite of an infected *Anopheles* mosquito, mostly in sub-Saharan Africa | By swallowing eggs that have matured in soil contaminated with faeces, where sanitation is poor, in the tropics and subtropics, including parts of South-East Asia |
| Which stage causes disease? | The blood stage: bursting red cells cause fever, and their loss causes anaemia | Adult worms in the small intestine: heavy infections obstruct the intestine and impair children's nutrition (see [*Helminths*](helminths.qmd)); larvae passing through the lungs cause cough and wheeze |
| Which stage is found in the laboratory? | Parasites inside red cells on a blood film; a parasite protein in an antigen test | Eggs in the stool, once the adults have matured and begun to lay |
| Where can control break the cycle? | Bed nets and insecticides; prompt treatment; drugs for travellers; a vaccine for young children | Latrines; washing hands and raw vegetables; treating whole school-age populations at regular intervals |

## Detection, control and drug targets {#sec-life-practice}

### Finding the parasite {#sec-life-detect}

A test can find a parasite only in a sample that contains one of its stages, taken when that stage is
there. Protozoa and helminth eggs are large enough to see with a light microscope, so microscopy is
still a main test for parasites (see [*Detecting and controlling
microbes*](../foundations/detection-control.qmd#sec-det-kinds)). The life cycle shows which sample to
take:

- Parasites that live in the blood are seen in a stained blood film, as *P. falciparum* is seen
  inside red cells.
- Parasites that live in the gut leave eggs, cysts or larvae in the stool, as *A. lumbricoides* leaves
  its eggs. These are not passed evenly from day to day, so one negative stool sample does not exclude
  infection, and samples from several days may be examined.
- Parasites hidden in tissue leave nothing in the blood or stool to see. They are often detected by
  serology, the detection of the patient's antibodies as evidence of exposure (see [*Detecting and
  controlling microbes*](../foundations/detection-control.qmd#sec-det-serology)).

::: {.example}
Larvae of *Toxocara*, a roundworm of dogs and cats, wander through human tissues after a child
swallows its eggs from soil, but they cannot mature in a human and lay no eggs, so the stool shows
nothing and the infection is detected by serology (see [*Helminths*](helminths.qmd)).
:::

A sample taken at the wrong point in the cycle can miss the parasite even when the right sample is
chosen.

::: {.example}
While *A. lumbricoides* larvae pass through the lungs, causing cough and wheeze, a stool sample shows
no eggs: eggs appear only when the adults have matured in the intestine, two to three months after
the eggs were swallowed.
:::

Antigen tests and nucleic acid amplification tests (NAATs), which copy a stretch of the parasite's DNA
until it can be detected, find parasite molecules instead of the parasite itself. An antigen test
needs no microscope, and a NAAT can detect parasites too few to see, but like every NAAT it reports
only the organisms it was designed to detect (see [*Detecting and controlling
microbes*](../foundations/detection-control.qmd#sec-det-molecular)).

### Breaking the cycle {#sec-life-control}

Each link in a life cycle is a point at which it can be broken, as each link in the chain of infection
is (see [*Transmission, outbreaks and One
Health*](../foundations/transmission-outbreaks.qmd#sec-trans-chain)). The measure follows from the
link:

| Link in the cycle | Measure | Parasites it acts against |
|---|---|---|
| The vector | Bed nets treated with insecticide; insecticide sprayed on the inside walls of homes; removing standing water in which mosquito larvae develop | *P. falciparum* |
| Faeces reaching soil, water or food | Latrines and sewage treatment; safe drinking water; keeping untreated human faeces off fields; washing hands and raw vegetables | *A. lumbricoides*, *G. duodenalis* |
| Larvae in meat | Cooking meat thoroughly | *Taenia* tapeworms |
| Larvae in soil | Wearing footwear | Hookworms |
| Infected people, the source of new infections | Prompt treatment; treating whole school-age populations for worms at regular intervals | *P. falciparum*, *A. lumbricoides* |
| The person at risk | Drugs taken by travellers to prevent disease; vaccines against the sporozoite for young children in parts of Africa (see [*Detecting and controlling microbes*](../foundations/detection-control.qmd#sec-det-prevent)) | *P. falciparum* |

Treating whole populations of school-age children works against worms because the worms do not
multiply in the host: removing most of them removes most of the harm, even if a few remain. The
treatment does not reach the eggs in the soil, so where sanitation is unchanged the children are
reinfected and the treatment has to be repeated.

### What parasites have that human cells lack {#sec-life-targets}

Protozoa and helminths are eukaryotes, so they share most of their machinery with human cells and
offer fewer targets for drugs than bacteria do (see [*The microbial
world*](../foundations/microbial-world.qmd#sec-world-kinds)). A drug can harm a parasite without
harming the patient only by acting on something the parasite has and human cells lack:

| Parasite | What the parasite has | What human cells have instead | Drugs that act on it |
|---|---|---|---|
| *P. falciparum* | Enzymes that make its own folate | No folate synthesis: they take folate from the diet | Drugs that block folate synthesis |
| *P. falciparum* | A way to dispose of the haem released as it digests the haemoglobin of its red cell: it packs the haem, which is toxic to it, into harmless crystals | No such process | Drugs that stop the crystals forming, so that free haem poisons the parasite |
| Helminths | Worm-specific nerve and muscle ion channels | Different channels, which the drugs affect far less | Drugs that act on these channels and paralyse the worm, which is then expelled from the gut |
| Helminths | Worm tubulin, the protein of the worm's microtubules | Human tubulin, which these drugs bind far less tightly | Drugs that bind worm tubulin, used in school deworming |

Resistance arises in parasites, as in bacteria, by mutation and selection. Falciparum malaria is
therefore usually treated with a combination of drugs that act in different ways, so that a parasite
resistant to one is killed by another, as in the treatment of HIV infection (see [*Detecting viruses
and antiviral targets*](../viruses/detecting-viruses.qmd#sec-vdet-resistance)).
